**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0760), Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections. All the questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Regle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections » (3 sections : A 1800-1922, B 1922-1961, C 1961 to present, 4 questions chacune, numerotation continue 1 a 12). `regles_choix` porte le minimum impose, une regle `parmi 1 sur 4` par section ; la regle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable et est recopiee dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question est imprimee « (25 marks) » et la page de garde dit « All the questions carry equal marks » ; `points` de l'exercice et de la question unique valent 25. Aucun ecart avec le sujet (4 x 25 = 100).

Defauts d'impression du sujet : scan de deux pages (CamScanner) avec filigrane gcerevision.com et bandeau publicitaire, sans incidence sur la lecture, mais avec une legere transparence de texte (verso) en haut de la page 2 et entre quelques questions ; les intitules de section sont imprimes avec un tiret demi-cadratin (« 1800 - 1922 ») recopie avec un tiret simple ; la question 2 est imprimee « succeed to extend » (tournure incorrecte, recopiee telle quelle) ; la question 3 est ambigue (« the results of German annexation by 1884 ») ; la question 6 est maladroite (« indigenous resistance and failure against French rule »). Aucune figure, carte ni document dans le sujet. Page de garde verifiee : ADVANCED LEVEL, History 2, Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, code 0760, JUNE 2026 (reference GCE26/0760/2/BN).

Aucun corrige officiel : les corriges sont des reponses modeles redigees de memoire, sans acces a une source. Les dates, noms et traites sont ceux de l'historiographie etablie ; les faits dont la precision est moindre sont formules prudemment ou sans chiffre. Aucune citation, statistique ni source n'est inventee. Les corriges sont a relire par un historien du Cameroun avant diffusion.

Question 11 : dates selon l'historiographie courante (annonce par Ahidjo le 6 mai 1972, referendum du 20 mai 1972, promulgation de la Constitution de la Republique unie du Cameroun le 2 juin 1972, retour au nom « Republique du Cameroun » en 1984). Le taux d'approbation du referendum n'est pas chiffre. L'hypothese petroliere (les decouvertes de petrole au large de la region occidentale) est mentionnee comme une explication avancee par certains critiques, sans l'affirmer. A faire relire par un historien du Cameroun si diffusion.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Examine the motives for and the effects of the dissolution of the Cameroon Federation in 1972.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The federation created in 1961 was ended in 1972. On 6 May 1972 President Ahmadou Ahidjo announced a referendum on a new constitution; the referendum of 20 May 1972 was approved by a very large majority, and on 2 June 1972 the unitary United Republic of Cameroon replaced the Federal Republic. West Cameroon and East Cameroon ceased to be federated states. This answer examines why Ahidjo ended the federation and what the consequences were.

**1. The motives.**
(a) *National unity and integration.* The official argument was that Cameroon was one nation, and that federalism, which maintained two states with different institutions, laws and languages, was a legacy of colonial rule that kept alive differences. Unity needed one state.
(b) *Economic and administrative efficiency.* Ahidjo argued that the two state governments, parliaments and administrations were costly and duplicated each other. A single central administration would save money and make planning and development easier, in the context of the national five-year plans.
(c) *The wish to strengthen presidential power.* Ahidjo's critics saw the change as a step in the concentration of power already shown by the creation of the single party, the Cameroon National Union (CNU), in 1966 and by the control of the federated states through federal inspectors. Abolishing the federation removed the last institutions that could limit the President.
(d) *Political context.* After the Nigerian civil war (1967-1970) the fear of secession and of ethnic fragmentation made leaders wary of any structure that could encourage separatism; a unitary state was seen as safer. The success of the single party and the weakening of the opposition made the move easier.
(e) *Pressure from the French-speaking majority and the elite.* Many people from the more populous East favoured a unitary state, and parts of the political class argued that federalism was an obstacle.
(f) *Economic interests.* Some critics suggest that control over the resources of the West, including the offshore oil then being discovered and developed, was a hidden motive; this is an interpretation, not a proven fact.
(g) *Weak opposition.* West Cameroon leaders, bound by the single party, were in no position to resist. The referendum was held in a situation where the opposition had no real voice.

**2. The effects.**
(a) *Political effects.* The federal and state institutions disappeared: the West Cameroon House of Assembly, the Prime Minister and the House of Chiefs were abolished, and the former federated states were divided into provinces (the North-West and South-West provinces), run by governors appointed by the President. The Constitution of 1961, which required the consent of the West Cameroon deputies to a change in the federal structure, was not respected. The President received much wider powers, and the state became highly centralised.
(b) *Effects on the Anglophone community.* Anglophones lost their own institutions and felt that their identity, their political voice, and their traditions of common law and of education were being eroded. The change fed the sense of marginalisation and was a root of what later became known as the "Anglophone problem" (the 1993 All Anglophone Conference, the creation of the GCE Board in 1993, and the crisis that began in 2016).
(c) *Symbolic effects.* The new name "United Republic of Cameroon" and the replacement of 1 October by 20 May as the national day, and, later, the renaming of the state "Republic of Cameroon" by President Biya in 1984 (the name of the former French Cameroun), were seen by some as the loss of the union's meaning.
(d) *Administrative and economic effects.* A single administration, legal system and budget were established; costs were reduced at the top and national planning was centralised. West Cameroon became more dependent on Yaoundé for its funding and development.
(e) *Strengthening the regime.* The end of federalism consolidated the position of the President and of the single party, and prepared a political system in which power came from the centre until the reforms of the 1990s.
(f) *Unity and integration.* Supporters point to a more integrated country and say that national institutions allowed the state to focus on development and to promote national unity, and that the people of the two former states mixed more.

**3. Assessment.** The dissolution was justified in terms of national unity and economic efficiency, but it was also a political decision to centralise power taken without genuine consultation of West Cameroon. Its effects were to strengthen the central government and national integration, at the cost of the autonomy and identity of the Anglophone minority, which remains a source of tension.

**Conclusion.** The federation was dissolved in 1972 for reasons of unity, cost and efficiency, and because Ahidjo wanted to concentrate power. The result was a centralised unitary state, more powerful presidency and a lasting Anglophone grievance.
